metaDescription: Six cordless impact drivers compared on torque, speed, noise and battery platform, with picks for framing, decks, tight spaces and light DIY.
expertTake: The DeWalt DCF845P1 is the impact driver to buy if you drive deck screws, lag bolts and structural fasteners regularly. The Craftsman CMCF800C1 is the value pick for a homeowner with a weekend of fastening ahead. If you mostly assemble furniture, skip impact drivers entirely and buy a standard drill, since the hammering action chews through small screw heads.
introParagraphs: An impact driver looks like a small drill, but it works differently. Inside, a spring loaded hammer strikes an anvil many times a second, so rotation arrives in short bursts instead of a steady push. That is why the quoted torque figure and the real feel of a tool in your hand often disagree.
This guide explains what torque, impacts per minute and brushless motors actually mean, how noise and size change daily use, and where cheap kits fall short.

products.name: DeWalt DCF845P1 20V MAX Brushless 3-Speed Impact Driver Kit
products.description:
The DCF845P1 is the benchmark: a brushless motor produces 1,825 in-lbs and 3,400 rpm, enough to bury 3 inch structural screws and drive lag bolts into framing. A three speed switch lets you drop to a low, controlled setting for small fasteners, which protects screw heads and soft materials. That range is what makes it work for both framing and finish carpentry.

Compared with the DCF787D1 it is more powerful but less compact, and against the Craftsman CMCF800C1's 1,460 in-lbs it has roughly 25 percent more torque. It is also louder than the DCF870B, because the conventional hammer and anvil is a noisy mechanism. For most buyers the extra torque is worth the cost, since stalled screws are the main cause of broken bits.

The kit includes a battery and charger, so it is ready on arrival. Replace worn bits regularly, because a rounded bit wastes the tool's torque, and keep the hex collet clean of dust.
products.bestFor: Carpenters and serious DIYers driving large screws every week.
pros: 1,825 in-lbs drives large structural screws
Three speed modes protect small fasteners
Brushless motor extends run time
Kit includes battery and charger
cons: Higher cost than light duty kits

products.name: DeWalt DCF787D1 20V MAX Compact Brushless Impact Driver Kit
products.description:
The DCF787D1 is the compact member of DeWalt's lineup. A brushless motor and short body let it reach into cabinets, between joists and under sinks, and the LED stays lit for 20 seconds after you release the trigger. It is the impact driver for people who value access over maximum torque.

The DCF845P1 outpowers it, and the compact size means less leverage for long lag screws. For typical household fasteners, deck screws and hinges it has plenty of power. Compared with the Craftsman CMCF800C1 it has a more refined motor and better trigger control.

It shares 20V MAX batteries with every other DeWalt tool, so adding a drill later is cheap. Because the hex collet takes standard 1/4 inch bits, use impact rated bits to avoid snapped tips.
products.bestFor: Remodelers and homeowners working in tight spaces.
pros: Compact body fits cabinets and framing bays
Brushless motor boosts run time
LED stays lit after trigger release
Uses the 20V MAX battery family

products.name: DeWalt DCF870B 20V MAX Hydraulic Impact Driver
products.description:
The DCF870B replaces the clanging hammer and anvil with a hydraulic mechanism that pushes through oil, so it is far quieter, up to 57 percent by the maker's claim. The same design keeps performance steady in cold weather. It is the pick for indoor work, early mornings or any job near sleeping neighbors.

The tradeoff is a more complex mechanism, and a higher price than the DCF845P1 conventional design. It also arrives as a bare tool, so you need to buy batteries and a charger if you do not own 20V MAX gear. For remodeling interiors it is a luxury many buyers will enjoy.

Hydraulic mechanisms need no routine oil changes by the owner, but a drop can damage the seals. Treat it like a precision tool rather than a hammer.
products.bestFor: Interior remodelers who want a quieter impact driver.
pros: Up to 57 percent quieter operation
Steady performance in cold weather
Brushless motor with fast driving
Extra comfortable in enclosed spaces

products.name: Craftsman CMCF800C1 20V MAX Impact Driver Kit
products.description:
The CMCF800C1 states 1,460 in-lbs, 2,800 rpm and 3,100 impacts per minute, and that is plenty for deck screws, fence hardware and general household fastening. The quick release chuck lets you change bits one handed. It is a straightforward impact driver without brushless motor refinement.

Compared with the DeWalt DCF845P1 it loses about 365 in-lbs of torque, which shows up when you push 3 inch screws into dense lumber. It is a better fit for the occasional user who needs a reliable tool at a lower price. Against the Black+Decker BDCI20C it offers somewhat higher torque.

You get a battery and charger in the kit, which keeps it simple. Keep an impact rated bit set on hand, and avoid using the tool as a drill with a chuck adapter for long periods.
pros: 1,460 in-lbs handles deck and fence screws
Quick release chuck allows one hand bit changes
LED lights the work area
Lower cost than DeWalt
cons: Less torque than DeWalt's top kits

products.name: Black+Decker BDCI20C 20V MAX Impact Driver Kit
products.description:
The BDCI20C quotes 1,375 in-lbs, 3,000 rpm and 3,900 impacts per minute, which is a respectable set of numbers for a tool aimed at light work. The extra impacts per minute help it seat screws quickly, even if the peak torque is lower than the DeWalt DCF845P1. It is compact and light enough to avoid wrist fatigue.

Compared with the Craftsman CMCF800C1 it has slightly lower torque but more impacts per minute. It is meant for household repairs, small decks and furniture projects. For long lag screws and structural framing, step up.

The battery is a Black+Decker 20V MAX type that powers a wide range of home tools. Store it at partial charge, and use bits designed for impact drivers so they do not shatter.
products.bestFor: First time buyers and light household tasks.
pros: 3,900 impacts per minute seats screws quickly
Compact and light for easy handling
Quick release chuck speeds bit swaps
Part of a broad home tool battery range
cons: Lower torque than pro grade drivers

products.name: GoYwato Brushless 21V Impact Driver Set with Two 4.0 Ah Batteries
products.description:
The GoYwato set advertises 2,655 in-lbs from a brushless motor and ships with two 4.0 Ah batteries and a set of sockets. A number that high should be read as a peak claim rather than a working figure, since it is well above the DeWalt DCF845P1's 1,825 in-lbs. Even at a lower real output, the two large batteries give long run time.

The value is in the kit contents: two big batteries and extras at a low price. Compared with the Craftsman CMCF800C1 it offers more battery capacity and a brushless motor, but no major brand support. Parts and service depend on the seller.

The battery platform is proprietary, so you cannot share packs with other brands. Check the warranty before purchase and avoid leaving the tool in hot vehicles.
products.bestFor: Budget buyers who want large batteries and a brushless motor.
pros: Two 4.0 Ah batteries extend run time
Brushless motor in a low cost kit
Includes sockets for extra uses
High advertised torque for light jobs
cons: Torque claim is a peak figure, not working output
Proprietary battery fits no other tools

buyingCriteria.explanation: Impact driver torque is measured at the moment of impact, and brands measure it differently. The DeWalt DCF845P1 quotes 1,825 in-lbs, the Craftsman CMCF800C1 1,460 and the Black+Decker BDCI20C 1,375. The GoYwato claims 2,655 in-lbs, a figure that should be treated as a marketing peak. Compare tools from the same brand, and prefer named torque numbers from major makers.

Brushless motors run cooler and use battery power more efficiently than brushed ones. The DeWalt DCF845P1, DCF787D1 and DCF870B and the GoYwato are brushless, while the Craftsman and Black+Decker kits use brushed motors. For occasional use, brushed is fine. For daily deck building, the run time gain pays for itself.

A compact head reaches into cabinets, between studs and under vanities. The DeWalt DCF787D1 is the compact option, while the DCF845P1 is larger and stronger. Buyers often choose the most powerful tool and then cannot fit it where they need to drive screws. Think about where you work, not only what you drive.

A hammer and anvil impact driver is loud, and long jobs indoors can be punishing. The DeWalt DCF870B uses a hydraulic mechanism that is up to 57 percent quieter. If you work in finished homes or near neighbors, noise is a real buying factor. Hearing protection is still sensible on the conventional models.

A drill bit is not meant for an impact driver, because impacts shatter standard bits. Use impact rated bits with a torsion zone. Even the strong DeWalt DCF845P1 wastes torque if a bit rounds off or slips. Spend a little on a good bit set.

A kit with a battery and charger works immediately, but a bare tool makes sense if you already own the platform. The DeWalt DCF870B is a bare tool, while the DCF845P1 and Craftsman kit include batteries. The GoYwato comes with two 4.0 Ah batteries but no ecosystem. Think of platform lock-in as part of the price.

specDecoder.meaning: Inch pounds measure the twisting force at the moment of impact. A figure near 1,800 in-lbs, like the DCF845P1, is typical of strong 20V drivers. Torque describes how hard a screw can be driven.
specDecoder.watchFor: The GoYwato claim of 2,655 in-lbs exceeds the best DeWalt figure, which suggests a peak number.

specDecoder.meaning: Impacts per minute counts the hammer strikes. More strikes can seat a screw faster. The Black+Decker BDCI20C quotes 3,900 ipm, and the Craftsman CMCF800C1 quotes 3,100 ipm.
specDecoder.watchFor: A higher ipm does not mean more torque, since each strike may be lighter.

specDecoder.meaning: Speed with nothing attached. The DCF845P1 reaches 3,400 rpm. High speed drives small screws quickly.
specDecoder.watchFor: Speed under load is lower, and torque falls as rpm rises.

specDecoder.meaning: A mechanism that uses oil to cushion each strike. The DCF870B uses it to cut noise and vibration. It feels smoother than a hammer and anvil.
specDecoder.watchFor: More complex mechanisms cost more and tolerate drops less well.

specDecoder.meaning: Battery capacity. Two 4.0 Ah packs, as in the GoYwato kit, run far longer than one small pack. Weight rises with capacity.
specDecoder.watchFor: Large packs on a weak tool do not add power, only run time.

howWeEvaluated.title: Torque and speed
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared stated torque and speed, including 1,825 in-lbs on the DeWalt DCF845P1 and 1,460 in-lbs on the Craftsman. We treated unusually high claims such as the GoYwato's as peak numbers. Three speed control earned extra credit.

howWeEvaluated.title: Motor and mechanism
howWeEvaluated.description: We rewarded brushless motors and noted the DCF870B's hydraulic mechanism. Brushed tools lost points for run time but not for light use. Mechanism noise was a factor for indoor work.

howWeEvaluated.title: Size and handling
howWeEvaluated.description: Short body length and low weight matter in cabinets and framing bays. The DCF787D1 was ranked for access, and the DCF845P1 for power. Grip comfort and light placement were considered.

howWeEvaluated.title: Kit contents and platform
howWeEvaluated.description: We counted batteries and chargers in each kit and judged the platform. DeWalt 20V MAX and Craftsman V20 offer wide tool ranges, while the GoYwato battery fits only its own tools. Kit value mattered.

howWeEvaluated.title: Lineup positioning
howWeEvaluated.description: The DCF845P1 leads for torque and control, the DCF787D1 for compactness and the DCF870B for quiet. The Craftsman is the value choice and the Black+Decker the light duty choice. The GoYwato is the budget kit with large batteries.

cards.label: Brushless
cards.text: Electronics replace brushes, giving more efficiency and run time. The DeWalt DCF845P1, DCF787D1, DCF870B and GoYwato are brushless.

cards.label: Brushed
cards.text: Carbon brushes are simple and cheap. The Craftsman CMCF800C1 and Black+Decker BDCI20C use them, which is fine for light use.

howToChoose.note: Frequent users should choose brushless. Occasional users can save with a brushed kit.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: High torque, a three speed switch and a long run time. Deck screws are long and driven in dense wood. Corrosion resistant screws also need steady control to avoid cam out.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The DeWalt DCF845P1 is best, with its 1,825 in-lbs and speed modes. The Craftsman CMCF800C1 is a value alternative for a small deck. The GoYwato adds battery capacity for long days.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You work daily, drive large screws or need quiet. The DeWalt DCF845P1 or DCF870B repay the cost.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You fasten occasionally. The Craftsman CMCF800C1 and Black+Decker BDCI20C are enough.

maintenance.why: A worn bit slips and wastes torque. It also damages screw heads.
Dust prevents bits from locking. Wipe and blow it out.
A dirty trigger loses fine control. Blow out dust from the vents.
Partial charge indoors extends life. Avoid hot vehicles.

maintenance.task: Avoid chuck adapters for long drilling
maintenance.why: Impact mechanisms wear faster under continuous drilling. Use a drill for holes.

faq.a: Use a drill for holes and delicate screws. Use an impact driver for large screws and fasteners. Many owners buy both as a combo kit.
For regular use, yes, since it gives more run time and less heat. For occasional work a brushed tool is fine.

faq.q: How much torque do I need?
faq.a: Around 1,400 in-lbs suits household use, and 1,800 in-lbs suits deck building and framing. Higher numbers from unknown brands may be peak claims.

faq.q: Why is my impact driver so loud?
faq.a: The hammer and anvil strikes produce the noise. A hydraulic design like the DeWalt DCF870B is quieter.

faq.q: Can I use regular drill bits?
faq.a: Not safely. Impacts shatter standard bits, so use impact rated bits and sockets.

faq.q: Can I drill holes with an impact driver?
faq.a: Yes with hex shank bits, but it is rougher than a drill and not ideal for precision.
